title: Boyle's, Charles' and the General Gas Law

blocks.text: Leave a sealed plastic bottle in a parked car in Maiduguri at midday and it swells; bring it into an air-conditioned room and it collapses inwards. Nothing entered or left the bottle. The gas laws describe exactly how much it should swell, and by how much it should shrink.

blocks.markdown:
## Three variables, three laws

A fixed mass of gas is described by three quantities: pressure P, volume V and absolute temperature T. Each classic gas law holds one of them constant and relates the other two.

blocks.title: Boyle's law
blocks.text: At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. That is PV is constant, so P1V1 = P2V2. Squeeze a gas into half the volume and its pressure doubles.

blocks.title: Charles' law
blocks.text: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. That is V divided by T is constant, so V1/T1 = V2/T2. Double the kelvin temperature and the volume doubles.

blocks.caption: The general gas equation combines Boyle's law and Charles' law

blocks.title: Kelvin, always
blocks.text: Every gas law uses absolute temperature. Convert with T in kelvin = temperature in degrees Celsius + 273. Using degrees Celsius directly gives a badly wrong answer and can even produce a negative volume. Standard temperature and pressure, s.t.p., means 273 K and 760 mmHg, which is 1 atmosphere or 101325 Pa.

blocks.markdown:
### Why the laws work — kinetic theory

- **Boyle's law**: reducing the volume packs the same number of molecules into a smaller space, so they strike each unit area of the wall more often. More collisions per second means higher pressure.
- **Charles' law**: raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the gas must expand to keep the pressure constant.

blocks.title: Converting a gas volume to s.t.p.
blocks.prompt: A sample of gas occupies 200 cm3 at 27 degrees Celsius and 750 mmHg. Calculate its volume at s.t.p.

steps.text: List the two sets of conditions. Initially P1 = 750 mmHg, V1 = 200 cm3, and T1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
At s.t.p. P2 = 760 mmHg and T2 = 273 K, and V2 is what we want.
Write the general gas equation and rearrange for V2.
Evaluate the numerator: 750 x 200 = 150000, and 150000 x 273 = 40 950 000.
Sanity check: the pressure rose slightly and the temperature fell, and both changes shrink a gas, so a result below 200 cm3 is exactly what we expect.

blocks.caption: The gas laws at a glance

blocks.title: Predict the direction before you calculate
blocks.text: Decide in advance whether the volume should rise or fall. Higher pressure or lower temperature shrinks a gas; lower pressure or higher temperature expands it. If your calculated answer moves the wrong way you have inverted a fraction, and you can catch it before submitting.

points: Boyle's law: at constant temperature P1V1 = P2V2.
Charles' law: at constant pressure V1/T1 = V2/T2.
The general gas equation P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 covers any change in a fixed mass of gas.
Temperature must always be converted to kelvin by adding 273 to the Celsius value.
Standard temperature and pressure is 273 K and 760 mmHg, that is one atmosphere.
Kinetic theory explains the laws through the frequency and force of molecular collisions with the walls.
